title: Polynomial kernels for Boolean MinCSP
formal: Classify all fixed finite Boolean constraint languages \(\Gamma\) for which \(\operatorname{MinCSP}(\Gamma)\), parameterized by the allowed number \(k\) of violated constraints, admits a randomized polynomial kernel. Equivalently, determine the membership function \(\chi_{\mathrm{ker}}(\Gamma)\in\{0,1\}\) of this class for every finite Boolean language. Deterministic kernels also qualify; the target retains the full language classification and the allowance for randomization in PACS 2024 Question 9.
why: This would classify the full preprocessing power of finite Boolean constraint languages after the fixed-parameter solvability boundary is known. It asks which nearly satisfiable systems admit a compact equivalent core whose size depends only polynomially on the repair budget. The source allows randomization so that the classification addresses this compression boundary without also demanding derandomization of established kernels.
status_note: The July 2024 workshop poses the full polynomial-kernel classification. The April 2025 full dichotomy manuscript still treats it as a future classification, and the checked SWAT 2026 theorem concerns a different preprocessing guarantee. Bounded primary-source searches on 15 September 2026 found no full kernelization classification. This is a sourced open-status assessment, not an exhaustive proof that no later resolution exists.

progress.text: Kratsch and Wahlström establish a randomized polynomial kernel for Almost 2-SAT; the result appears in JACM in 2020.

The flow-augmentation work classifies fixed-parameter tractability of Boolean MinCSP and its weighted variant; the April 2025 full revision still identifies kernelizability as a separate classification direction.
PACS Question 9 asks for this language-wide polynomial-kernel classification and explicitly permits randomized kernels and standard complexity assumptions.
Jansen and Verhaegh classify essential-constraint detection, a different preprocessing task, and distinguish kernelization by solution cost from variable-based compression.

sentences: Boolean MinCSP asks whether an assignment can violate at most a specified number of constraints.
The question seeks all finite Boolean languages admitting polynomial kernels in that violation budget.
A kernel must run in polynomial time and output a same-problem instance with polynomially many parameter-dependent bits.
Randomization is allowed, and the recorded complexity assumption may support lower bounds for the excluded languages.
A classification would reveal which nearly feasible constraint systems admit efficient compression beyond their known fixed-parameter algorithms.

definitions:
A finite Boolean constraint language \(\Gamma\) is a finite list of named relations \(R\subseteq\{0,1\}^{r}\), each of positive integer arity \(r\), described by its complete finite table. Empty relations, full relations and the empty language are allowed. For each individual decision problem \(\Gamma\) is fixed, including its maximum arity. There is no global bound on arity or on the number of relations when classifying languages.

An instance is \((F,k)\), where \(k\in\mathbb N\) and \(F\) is a finite set of constraints \(R(x_1,\ldots,x_{r})\) on variables \(V=\{1,\ldots,n\}\), with \(n\geq0\). Coordinates may repeat. The set convention follows §1.1 of the cited dichotomy; repeated listings of the identical named constraint do not create extra cost. An assignment \(a:V\to\{0,1\}\) violates a constraint when \((a(x_1),\ldots,a(x_{r}))\notin R\). Let \(\operatorname{opt}_\Gamma(F)\) be the minimum number of violated constraints over all assignments. The instance is yes exactly when \(\operatorname{opt}_\Gamma(F)\leq k\), equivalently when deleting at most \(k\) constraints makes the rest satisfiable. All constraints have unit cost and may be deleted; there are no separately undeletable constraints or freely supplied constant assignments.

Use an explicit binary input encoding: unary \(n\) and constraint count, each followed by zero; each constraint has a relation index in the fixed language and a tuple of variable indices of width \(\lceil\log_2(n+1)\rceil\); finish with the length-prefixed binary representation of \(k\). The full length \(L\) includes isolated variables and the parameter bits. Output instances use the same convention. Encodings can be normalized to remove duplicate constraints in polynomial time.

A randomized polynomial kernel for a fixed \(\Gamma\) is a probabilistic multitape Turing machine \(K_\Gamma\) using independent fair coin flips, with no oracle or advice. There are positive integer constants \(C,d,e\), depending on \(\Gamma\) only, such that on every valid input \((F,k)\), and for every sequence of coin outcomes, it halts within \(C(L+1)^{e}\) bit steps and outputs a valid instance \((F',k')\) of the same \(\operatorname{MinCSP}(\Gamma)\) with total encoding length at most \(C(k+1)^{d}\). Require
\[\Pr\bigl[\operatorname{opt}_\Gamma(F)\leq k\ \Longleftrightarrow\ \operatorname{opt}_\Gamma(F')\leq k'\bigr]\geq 2/3.\]
This is a worst-case guarantee for each input over the kernel's internal randomness; both kinds of error are allowed. The original workshop permits randomized kernels without fixing an error convention; bounded two-sided error and an all-runs size bound are recorded here explicitly. A deterministic kernel has probability one. The machine may create new variables and constraints from the same fixed language. It need not preserve the optimum or the entire solution set, and need not be a subformula reduction.

Define \(\chi_{\mathrm{ker}}(\Gamma)=1\) if such a machine and constants exist, and \(0\) otherwise. Its classification is over all finite language tables. No uniform machine for recognizing the class is demanded. A polynomial kernel is different from an algorithm taking \(f(k)(L+1)^{e}\) time for an arbitrary computable function \(f\), and from a compression to an instance of a different decision problem. A bound in the variable count \(n\) alone is not a bound in the parameter \(k\).

The source allows standard complexity assumptions for the lower-bound side. This card fixes the customary hypothesis \(\mathrm{NP}\not\subseteq\mathrm{coNP}/\mathrm{poly}\) as an admissible conditional premise. Here \(\mathrm{NP}\) consists of binary languages with polynomially bounded certificates verifiable by deterministic polynomial-time machines. A language is in \(\mathrm{NP}/\mathrm{poly}\) when such a verifier may also receive an arbitrary advice string of polynomial length depending only on input length; advice need not be computable. A language is in \(\mathrm{coNP}/\mathrm{poly}\) when its complement is in \(\mathrm{NP}/\mathrm{poly}\). The stated noncontainment means that some NP language lacks such a complement verifier. It is an assumption, not a proved theorem or a conclusion automatically obtained from any parameterized hardness result.
answer_criterion: Give a substantive mathematical characterization, represented by a real-valued function \(g\) on all finite Boolean languages, and prove in Lean that \(|g(\Gamma)-\chi_{\mathrm{ker}}(\Gamma)|\leq1/100\) for every \(\Gamma\). An exact necessary-and-sufficient classification also qualifies. For every class identified as admitting a kernel, establish the stated machine, runtime, size and per-input error guarantees without an unproved assumption. For every excluded class, prove nonexistence of such a randomized kernel either unconditionally or under the explicitly stated hypothesis \(\mathrm{NP}\not\subseteq\mathrm{coNP}/\mathrm{poly}\), labelling the classification conditional when used. The required lower bounds must cover the allowed randomized model. Merely renaming the defining kernel-existence predicate, classifying only fixed-parameter tractability, excluding only deterministic kernels, or solving finitely many languages does not settle the question. No algorithm efficiently recognizing the class from language tables is required.

source_formulation.text: For which Boolean constraint languages can instances be reduced in polynomial time to equivalent instances of size polynomial in the permitted number of unsatisfied constraints, allowing randomized reductions and standard conditional lower bounds?
source_formulation.caption: Editorial paraphrase of PACS 2024 Question 9

context_blocks.text: A small number of violated constraints represents a small repair to an otherwise feasible system. Fixed-parameter tractability permits expensive work that depends only on that repair budget. A polynomial kernel asks instead for polynomial-time preprocessing that compresses all subsequent difficulty into a number of bits bounded polynomially in the budget. These demands can have different boundaries.

Almost 2-SAT is the language consisting of all Boolean clauses with at most two literals, viewed as individual relations. Its randomized polynomial kernel is an established positive example. The workshop includes it explicitly to allow randomization; requiring deterministic kernels would add a further unresolved issue from that example.

The completed FPT dichotomy of Kim, Kratsch, Pilipczuk and Wahlström distinguishes which Boolean MinCSPs admit algorithms with parameter-dependent overhead. It also distinguishes weighted and unweighted variants. This card uses the unweighted problem and asks the subsequent preprocessing classification, which their revised manuscript still presents as a further question.

The SWAT 2026 essential-constraint theorem concerns identifying constraints that occur in all sufficiently good repair sets. That preprocessing can improve the effective search parameter, but does not assert that the entire instance shrinks to polynomial size in the original violation budget. The same paper distinguishes results about compression measured by the number of variables.
